2.0.s.en: 1. His prayer in the belly of the fish:

2.0.0.en: 1 Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly. Who among us can express the distress into which Jonah entered?! In the belly of the fish Jonah descended into affliction as into a tomb, in which his own thoughts, abilities and resources died; he did not know what to do, nor could he foresee what would befall him. The fish would float on the waters, and Jonah would breathe air and see a glimmer of light; it would take him down into the waters, and he would find himself in pitch darkness. The fish would open its mouth, and Jonah would be drowned in salt water; the fish would expel the water, and Jonah would recover his breath. So Jonah lived a few days; were it not for God's care for him and His favors toward him, every second of them would have been a heavy mountain crushing his soul, and death would have become for him a desire.

2.0.1.en: In any case, in his affliction Jonah was joined to the Lord buried in the tomb, through type and shadow, and so he set out with his heart and mind not to the outside of the fish but to what is above the place; he rose up to God praying as one in a heavenly sanctuary, for it says: “Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly” [1].

2.0.2.en: Before, he called the Lord “the God of heaven” (Jon 1:9), but in affliction it says “the LORD his God”... The Lord is attributed to Jonah as his God. He is the God of the afflicted and the suffering, as though He leaves His heavens and comes down to Jonah to support him in his distress, or, in other words, He turns his life into a heaven in which the Lord his God dwells, so He is called his God, that is, the God of the heavens in which He dwells. Our God is the God of Jonah the sufferer who carries the Cross, the God of every embittered soul; He enters him so that he may be called “the God of heaven”... for He makes of those who carry the Cross holy heavens.

2.0.3.en: Jonah gave us his wonderful prayer, indeed his unique prophetic hymn, not in moments of ease, nor inside the temple building as a teacher, but in the midst of sufferings as one in the tomb of the crucified Lord Christ. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us not be concerned with the place but with the Lord of the place, for Jonah was in the belly of the fish and the Lord listened to his prayer. And you, even if you are in the baths, pray. Wherever you are, pray; do not seek a place in which to pray, for your soul is a temple].

2.0.4.en: If the Church is concerned even with the building, that it may be an icon of heaven, it is so that we may bear the marks of heaven in us, and look to the inner spiritual building, and our eyes may be lifted to the holy things that the Holy Spirit establishes in us, especially in moments of affliction and pain!

2.0.5.en: Affliction is the Golgotha in which we enjoy being crucified with our Lord Jesus, that we may go forth with Him to His glories and be with Him and in Him in the bosom of the heavenly Father by His Holy Spirit.

2.1.0.en: 2 And said, “I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice. 3 For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me. 4 Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple. 5 The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head. 6 I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God. 7 When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.

2.1.1.en: “I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice” [2].

2.1.2.en: When Jonah was cast into the salt waters he entered the belly of the fish, not to see death with his eyes but to behold, through the shadow, the Lord Christ Himself cast into affliction with us and for us, so that when He cries out with His blameless life the Father answers Him and lifts us with Him above affliction. The One who is without blemish came down to our lowliness that we might become in Him the object of the Father's pleasure, that He might hear us in our affliction and lift us up to Himself. As St. Jerome says: [The Lord came down; for our sake He humbled Himself, that we might ascend in safety and confidence].

2.1.3.en: Jonah called on the Lord in his affliction and enjoyed the answer at once, for he saw himself ascending not from the belly of the fish but from the belly of hell in Christ Jesus crucified! Here he speaks in the past tense, not the future: “he heard me,” “thou heardest my voice,” the form of true enjoyment through the type, and the form of certainty that carries no doubt.

2.1.4.en: The prophet Jeremiah bore the same feelings and grasped the same concepts when he was cast into the pit, for he said: “I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon. Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry” (Lam 3:55-56).

2.2.0.en: “For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about” [3].

2.2.1.en: Jonah realized that it was God who cast him into the deep, in the midst of the seas, and not the mariners. But the wonder is that when he went down even to the depths he did not find himself under the weight of the pressure of the seas' waters and their dangers, but found himself surrounded by a holy river that waters him and gladdens him with abundant spiritual fruit, the river of which it is said in the Psalm: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Ps 46:4). In the midst of bitter affliction, “In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul”; instead of the bitter salt waters I have the sweet waters of the river, and instead of the weight of the waters upon me, the waters surround me for delight and joy.

2.2.2.en: What is the midst of the seas into which Jonah was cast? It is the depths of the bitter Cross, which the Lord Christ entered as a propitiatory sacrifice for the whole world, and through it He caused the sweet, life-giving waters of Baptism to burst forth, so that a river surrounded Him, that is, His Church, which is His Body: the river of Baptism, that is, the waters of the Jordan. This sight drew the hearts of the prophets, so the prophet Ezekiel says about the Church of the New Testament, or the new temple: “Afterward he brought me again unto the door of the house; and, behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward... and the waters came down from under from the right side of the house, at the south side of the altar... a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over... for they shall come thither, and they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh... And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine” (Ezek 47).

2.2.3.en: Our sins cast the Lord Christ, in His love for us, into the midst of the seas, to bear the divine wrath for us through the Cross, turning the saltiness of the seas into the sweetness of rivers, so that He gives us in Him, through the Cross itself, the river of His Holy Spirit, who waters our souls and gives them fruit and grants them healing! Thus the Cross bore two complementary images: the image of God's wrath against sin, which cost the Lord His life, and the image of God's surpassing love, which caused the springs of His surpassing grace to burst forth.

2.2.4.en: St. Jerome says: [For the Savior the Lord, the image came in the Psalm: “I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me” (Ps 69:3), as it is said of Him in another Psalm: “But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground. Thou hast broken down all his hedges” (Ps 89:39)... And although He was in salt waters, being tempted in all things, yet they were not salt (bitter) for Him, for a river surrounded Him, as it is said in another place: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Ps 46:4)].

2.2.5.en: St. Ambrose speaks to us of this river that surrounds us as the Holy Spirit, who waters the heavenly Jerusalem, who overflowed upon the Church through Christ Jesus crucified. [The Holy Spirit is the river, the plentiful river, the great river that flows always without ceasing... For the heavenly Jerusalem is not watered by an earthly river but by the Holy Spirit].

2.2.6.en: Through the Cross we have enjoyed the river of the New Testament instead of the well of the Old Testament. As St. Ambrose says: [The Old Testament is a deep well from which water is drawn with effort; it was not full to the brim, but there came after it the One who says: “I am not come to destroy (the Law), but to fulfil” (Mt 5:17)... But the New Testament is not merely a river, but “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (Jn 7:38), rivers of understanding, rivers of contemplation, spiritual rivers]. Thus, when the Lord sits with us at the well, as with the Samaritan woman at noon, that is, in the moments of the Cross, He causes the springs of His waters to burst forth in us like living, gladdening rivers.

2.2.7.en: The prophet continues his hymn on the tongue of the Lord Christ, saying: “all thy billows and thy waves passed over me” [3]. St. Jerome comments on this phrase, saying: [Let us inquire how the billows and waves passed over the Savior... for there is no one able to endure all trials except the One who was tempted in all things... All the afflictions and toils that trouble the human race and that break all ships passed over His head... He endured the storm and all the turmoil so that others might be in calm!].

2.3.0.en: If the billows point to the judgments of God, as St. Cyril the Great says: [The Lord bore upon Himself all the judgments of God against us. All the judgments fell upon Him to be fulfilled in His body, as the Psalmist says: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Ps 42:7). Thus the Lord Christ appeared as the One who pays the debt, as one cast out from the eyes of the Father, although He is the Intercessor who carries His people into the heavenly sanctuaries. Therefore the prophet continues his speech: “Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple” [4].

2.3.1.en: It is a realistic picture of the Cross: on one side the Savior appeared as one cast out, crying out and saying: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46). On the other side, He bears humanity in His body that it may be glorified with Him. As St. Jerome says: [The Lord became as one in your position (cast out)... in order to lift humanity up to be with Him where He is (Jn 17:2)]. He carries out His work as the greatest High Priest, entering into the temple of His heavenly sanctuary, bearing His Church into the very heavenly places, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us” (Heb 9:24). So while He is cast out for our sake, He bears us in Him that we may be the object of the Father's good pleasure and delight.

2.3.2.en: Jonah was not a priest to enter the Holy Place, nor a high priest to enjoy the sight of the Holy of Holies once every year, but in the depths of the sea, when he became as one cast out, he was counted a type of the Lord Christ, who was cast out and entered His heavenly sanctuaries. As St. Jerome says: [In the depths of the sea he sees the temple of the Lord, and in the spirit of prophecy he found himself there contemplating something else].

2.4.0.en: “The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about... yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God” [5-6].

2.4.1.en: The Lord Christ descended into hell and became as one whom the waters compassed about, even to the soul, but the waters could not swallow Him; rather He frees those whom the waters had taken captive and drowned. He descended into the depths of the waters so that those drowned in them might ascend with Him, as the Apostle says: “Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph 4:9-10).

2.4.2.en: St. Augustine sees in the waters that compassed the Lord Christ, even to the soul, an expression of what happened at the Cross, for everyone rose against Him like the waves of the sea, and in His humility He submitted willingly for our sake, saying: “I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me” (Ps 69:2). He did not resist the violent words nor the cruel actions, but endured them patiently, and “became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8).

2.4.3.en: The Savior who walked on the waters (Mt 14:26) bent Himself down to the waters so that they would compass Him for a time and surround Him, that He might carry His believers over the waters through the ship of His Cross and bring them safely to the harbor of the heavenly Jerusalem.

2.5.0.en: Again he says: “When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple” [7]. Jonah lost all hope in a human arm for salvation, for he became as one seized in the belly of the fish, with no one to save him but the Lord; therefore he says: “I remembered the LORD.” It is as though he were with the Psalmist who says: “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” As St. Jerome says: [I found myself shut up in the bowels of the fish, so all my hope became in the Lord].

2.5.1.en: This phrase also applies to our suffering Jonah, who cried out in the flesh: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death” (Mt 26:38), “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mt 26:39). This burden that the Lord bore for our sake was so that He might carry out His priestly work through His propitiatory sacrifice and ask the Father on our behalf: “My prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.” As St. Jerome says: [As a priest He pleads for the deliverance of the people in His body].

2.6.0.en: “8 They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy. 9 But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of the LORD.” [8-9].

2.6.1.en: At the Cross there appeared those who observe lying vanities, those who followed the vanities of the Pharisees and so were deprived of the Lord Himself, their “mercy.” They were deprived of Christ their Savior and became like a satanic hymn that proclaims nothing but words of falsehood and blasphemy. But the Lord Christ, who was slandered, offered Himself as a hymn of thanksgiving to the Father, and a sacrifice of thanksgiving to Him.

2.6.2.en: If Jonah offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God in the belly of the fish, it was as a type of the Lord Christ, who saw everyone united against Him, and in love fulfilled His vow to the Father by offering His life as a ransom for many, even for His very tormentors!

2.6.3.en: In Christ Jesus the Sacrifice our whole life is turned into a harp in the hand of the Holy Spirit, singing a symphony of thanksgiving and gratitude to the Father, not with our mouths only but through all our conduct! If Jonah became a psalmist in the belly of the fish, it was to declare what the Lord Christ does in us through His sufferings, for He creates in us a nature of thanksgiving that touches our whole being, instead of the ingratitude that corrupted our life.

2.7.0.en: “And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.” [10].

2.7.1.en: St. John Chrysostom holds that God gave Jonah successive lessons in showing gentleness toward others: if the fish swallowed him and then cast him out without harming him, is it not fitting for him to show gentleness toward his brothers in humanity, even if they are Gentiles?! “The waves received him and did not choke him, and the fish caught him without destroying him... So it was fitting for the prophet to be gentle and merciful, and not to be harsher than the beast of prey or the ignorant mariners or the violent waves.

2.7.2.en: St. Jerome holds that the expression “vomited out” points to the victorious life coming out from where death is, for the belly of hell could not hold our Jonah, nor could corruption touch Him. As the Psalmist says: “For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Ps 16:10).

2.7.3.en: He rose from among the dead as the firstfruits for us, raising us with Him. As St. Jerome says: [He who died to free the captives from the bonds of death is able to lead many to life].
